title: DNS
subtitle: Hierarchical name resolution, record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, ALIAS), TTL caching trade-offs, Geo-DNS, and Anycast routing.
keyTakeaways: DNS resolution is a hierarchical recursive lookup spanning Root, Top-Level Domain (TLD), and Authoritative nameservers.
DNS TTL represents an architectural balance: high TTLs reduce client latency and nameserver load, while low TTLs enable rapid disaster recovery and traffic shifting.
Anycast DNS announces the same IP address from hundreds of worldwide data centers via BGP, routing users to the nearest geographical edge naturally.
architectureDiagram:
DNS RECURSIVE RESOLUTION FLOW
[ Client ] -> (1) Look in Local Cache / OS Resolver
                  |
                  v (Cache Miss)
[ Recursive Resolver ] ---> (2) Root Nameserver (".")
          |             <--- Returns ".com" TLD Server IP
          +---------------> (3) TLD Nameserver (".com")
          |             <--- Returns Authoritative Nameserver IP
          +---------------> (4) Authoritative Nameserver ("example.com")
                        <--- Returns A Record: 198.51.100.1 (TTL=300)

sections.heading: The Resolution Hierarchy and Core Record Types
sections.body: When a browser requests `api.example.com`, it triggers a hierarchical lookup across distributed servers. The OS resolver first checks its local cache. On a miss, it forwards the query to a recursive resolver (like Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` or Google's `8.8.8.8`). The recursive resolver queries the Root nameserver (which points to `.com` TLD servers), then queries the TLD nameserver (which points to `example.com` authoritative servers), and finally fetches the record from the authoritative nameserver.
bullets: A and AAAA Records: Maps a hostname directly to an IPv4 (32-bit) or IPv6 (128-bit) address.

CNAME vs ALIAS: CNAME maps a hostname to another hostname, but by RFC specification cannot be placed at the zone apex (`example.com`). ALIAS/ANAME records provide apex flattening by resolving to an IP address dynamically at query time.
NS and MX Records: NS delegates a DNS zone to authoritative nameservers; MX routes email traffic to designated mail exchanges.

codeSnippet.title: Standard Production DNS Configuration (BIND Syntax)
codeSnippet.code:
; Zone file for example.com
$TTL 300 ; Default 5-minute TTL for fast traffic shifting

@       IN  SOA   ns1.example.com. admin.example.com. (
                  2026100301 ; Serial
                  7200       ; Refresh
                  3600       ; Retry
                  1209600    ; Expire
                  300 )      ; Negative Cache TTL

@       IN  NS    ns1.cloudflare.com.
@       IN  NS    ns2.cloudflare.com.

; Apex apex ALIAS mapping to CloudFront CDN
@       IN  ALIAS d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net.

; Subdomain CNAME
api     IN  CNAME edge-lb.example.com.

sections.heading: Traffic Routing: Anycast vs Geo-DNS and the TTL Trap
sections.body: Global systems steer traffic using two primary DNS patterns: Geo-DNS and Anycast. Geo-DNS inspects the IP address of the client's recursive resolver to return an IP address physically near the user. Anycast advertises the exact same IP address from hundreds of globally distributed edge PoPs using BGP routing, allowing the internet's routing fabric to direct packets to the closest physical router.
bullets: The Geo-DNS Pitfall: Resolvers often sit hundreds of miles away from actual end users (e.g., corporate VPN resolvers or centralized public DNS), causing Geo-DNS to steer users to the wrong regional datacenter.
Anycast Routing Advantages: Fast automated failover; if a datacenter goes dark, BGP naturally withdraws the route and directs traffic to the next nearest PoP in seconds.

The TTL Dilemma: Setting TTL to 60 seconds allows instant failover during incidents, but increases DNS query latency and cost. Setting TTL to 24 hours cuts DNS traffic, but locks users onto dead IPs for a day if a datacenter fails.

tradeOffs.pros: Rapid traffic migration during disaster recovery; fast rollout of IP changes or blue/green infrastructure flips.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher query volume to authoritative nameservers; slight latency hit on initial visits; some ISP resolvers disregard low TTLs.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Critical production API load balancers, dynamic failover endpoints, and active cloud migrations.

tradeOffs.pros: Maximum cache hit ratio; near-zero DNS lookup latency for repeat users; protects nameservers from query spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Cannot perform emergency traffic diversion; IP changes take 24-48 hours to fully propagate worldwide.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Static marketing homepages, corporate email MX records, and stable root domain mappings.

interviewTip: Never rely on DNS for zero-downtime failover during a production outage. ISP and mobile carrier recursive resolvers frequently ignore low TTLs and cache records for hours. Use BGP Anycast routing or an edge CDN with health-checked origins for reliable failover.
